explanations.explanation: This neuron is acting like a “word‐ending” detector for multi-character or multi-syllable content words (especially in CJK text, but also in code names, list indices, Korean or English compounds).  It lights up on the final token of a semantically meaningful unit—e.g. the last character of a Chinese/Japanese noun (“会” in “大会,” “阵” in “矩阵,” “章” in “文章,” “答” in “回答,” etc.), the closing syllable of a Korean word (“레스” in “스트레스”), the end of a tab-label (“卡” in “选项卡2”), or the final element of a code identifier (“constant” in `tf.constant`), list number (“3.” in bullet lists), and so on.  In short, it marks the completion of a discrete lexical chunk.
This feature fires on the “end‐of‐heading” marker—i.e. the final punctuation or line‐break that terminates a section title or headline in articles, menus, wikis, etc.

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on the function words that introduce the object or subordinate clause in user-facing instructions, permissions and disclaimers—for example “the” in “Remove the…,” “see” in “tap here to see…,” “that” in license boilerplate, “cannot” in forum-permission messages, “Your” in form prompts, “All” in contribution notices, etc.
This neuron fires on the very first, capitalized word of a title, heading or menu label—i.e. the initial token of a headline‐style or section‐title string.

This neuron detects generic website UI boilerplate – the standard consent notices, form‐field prompts, share or navigation labels and error/disclaimer lines (e.g. cookie banners, “continue”/“assume” consent language, “enter your name/email,” “this video failed to load,” forum-permission messages, share-article buttons, license acknowledgments, etc.) that routinely frame primary page content.

This neuron fires on top‐level “header” or title/metadata lines that kick off a new document or section—e.g. court-opinion captions (docket numbers, “UNPUBLISHED”), class- or import-declares in code, article headlines and dates, paper titles, conference names, etc.

This feature fires on end-of-structure or “boundary” markers – the final element/key in a list or object (e.g. the third JSON property like “scale” or the last field “end”/“moniker”/“amount”), closing separators in prose or licenses (“***”), closing keywords (“end”), or other tokens that signal the tail or out-of-bounds end of a block or sequence.

This feature fires on the tokens that mark the start or end of logical blocks in mixed prose/code—that is, headings, import-or-using lines, config or comment section headers, and the punctuation ending them. It flags those structural boundary markers in documentation and code-like text.

This neuron picks up on the little “hedging‐and‐help” cues in a technical Q&A: modal/uncertainty markers (e.g. “possible,” “not sure”), polite-request pronouns (“someone,” “anyone”) and intensifiers/qualifiers (“really,” “completely,” “careful,” “highly”) that frame a request or caution in Stack-Overflow–style posts.

This neuron fires on the initial (often capitalized) subword of salient content words—proper names, acronyms, technical terms or morphological roots—marking the beginning of key entities and domain‐specific vocabulary.

This feature is a subword‐morpheme detector: it lights up on Latin/Greek‐derived root fragments (e.g. medi- in “intermediates,” ol- in Italian manipulazione, lic- in German Verpflichtung, rimin- in Diskriminierung, gr- in progressive, polit- in politiska, etc.) across different languages, marking the core semantic stems of those abstract nouns/adjectives.

This feature fires on title-case tokens that occur at the start (or in the headline) of a new segment—i.e. the first word or prominent word in a section title, headline or sentence (capitalized subword tokens marking section or title beginnings).

This feature fires on the little numbered/alphanumeric “call-outs” you see in scientific papers (section IDs, figure/table refs, bibliography tags like [@…], 15-078-15, 33-57, etc.). It captures the formatting of in-text citations and reference identifiers in academic prose.
This feature picks out the “.” token – i.e. the period/full stop – whenever it’s used (as a sentence terminator, a decimal‐point in numbers, an abbreviation dot or a dot in things like domain names).

This feature acts as a “segment‐start” detector: it lights up on the very first subtoken or punctuation of a new sentence, heading, dateline or code block—whether that’s a capitalized word‐prefix (“Vari,” “Integr,” “Dis,” “Ca”), a leading quote or bracket in Chinese/Japanese text, the initial period in acronyms or dotted identifiers (U.S., e.g., DOI), or the first token in an import/export line or section title.

This neuron lights up on “slot‐filler” tokens in semi-structured text—things like month names, numeric date/time pieces, list or section headings, acronyms and other domain-label keywords that serve as metadata or template fields.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is basically a “line‐start” detector.  It lights up on the very first non‐whitespace token after a newline—whether that’s the opening brace of a JS object, a comment marker (“//” or “#”), a horizontal rule, or the first character of a paragraph in any script (Chinese, Japanese, Hebrew, Thai, Russian, Tamil, Georgian, etc.).

This neuron seems to be flagging short character-chunks that occur as standalone subwords in hyphenated, slash-separated or compound identifiers (e.g. URL paths, chemical names, hyphenated numbers/units, transliterations, proper names, code imports, etc.). Essentially it lights up on those little pieces (“ino,” “oo,” “cc,” “ul,” “avan,” “vb,” “e,” etc.) that form discrete segments inside longer, often technical or foreign, multi-part tokens.

This feature fires on standalone alphanumeric “labels” in scientific/technical text—e.g. reference and section numbers, figure/table identifiers, and short domain‐specific codes (strain or protein designations, cell‐type abbreviations) that serve as structured markers rather than ordinary words.

This feature fires on the “head” of a nominal phrase—i.e. the central word that carries the phrase’s core meaning, whether that’s a noun (div, range, percent, frame, gas, part, cent, consisting), a determiner/possessor (his, their, its, own), or a numeral/determiner (one). It thus marks the semantic head of noun- or DP-type constituents across diverse contexts.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that serve as line-initial structural markers in technical or formal text—e.g. section headings (“Require…”/“Small…”), metadata keys or headers (“X-Account-Key:”, “;;” in licenses), markup delimiters (“#”, “{%”), docket/citation numbers (“893”, “476”, “5…”), class/type declarations, she-bangs, etc.—i.e. the prefixes that kick off new document sections or syntactic blocks.

This feature appears to mark “information‐unit” tokens – the little bits that introduce or quantify a new fact or segment.  Whether it’s a numeral (20, 763, 90, 14, 80 × , etc.), a small function word in various languages (Swedish aldrig, English an/s plural –s, German Mit, Danish antagelser), a domain label (Raman, Color), or a delimiter in structured data (commas, quotes) – it consistently fires on the token that kicks off a self‐contained piece of information across contexts.

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on the tokens that kick off a new structural or metadata block—anything that “opens” a section or declaration (e.g. an opening parenthesis in a list item, an XML/HTML tag name, an import/require or syntax directive, a comment-header/license line, a Markdown heading, etc.).

This feature fires on the “headline” or “label” tokens that kick off a new topic or domain‐specific term—often capitalized acronyms (FANCD2, GIT, GIP, FSA, Galpha), section/function names (f in math), or key news keywords (storm, debate, eliminatoria, vuelos, juez, fim) that signal a shift into a distinct subject area.

This neuron fires whenever the model is inside a parenthesized or otherwise delimited mini‐token—typically a short alphanumeric sequence like an abbreviation, code or identifier fragment (e.g. the “e” in “(i.e.),” a digit in an EC enzyme code, the “3” in “www.w3.org,” the “0” in a timestamp, the “dr” in a Swedish compound, “inf” in an XML namespace, “umer” in “enumerates,” “STRA” in “CONSTRAINT,” “to” in “up-to-date,” “include” in C++ directives, small numbers in chemical nomenclature, etc.). In other words, it marks those tiny subwords or symbol clusters that carry compact technical meaning inside parentheses or special syntactic frames.

This neuron fires on the very end of a standalone heading or title (menu labels, article headlines, section headers, etc.), effectively marking the boundary between that header text and the rest of the page.
